entries.label: Title and Edition Details
entries.summary: Title page information presenting Plato's Republic translated into English with introduction, analysis, and index by B. Jowett, in its revised third edition.

entries.label: Dedication to Former Pupils
entries.summary: Jowett inscribes the volume in gratitude to his former pupils at Balliol College and the University of Oxford across forty-six years.

entries.label: Editorial Acknowledgments
entries.summary: The translator acknowledges the assistance of Matthew Knight, Frank Fletcher, and J. W. Mackail for their scholarship, accuracy, index preparation, and correction of inaccuracies.

entries.label: Scope of Additions/Alterations
entries.summary: Additions and alterations made to both the introduction and the text affect at least one third of the work.

entries.label: Exchange Plan for 1881 Copies
entries.summary: Recognizing the extent of the revisions and the dissatisfaction of owning an inferior form, the translator arranged for owners of the 1881 edition to exchange clean copies for the new edition at half price.

entries.label: Future Dialogue Revisions
entries.summary: The translator expresses the hope to publish a revised edition of Plato's remaining dialogues within a year.

entries.label: Significance of the Republic
entries.summary: The Republic is celebrated as Plato's greatest dialogue, functioning as the center around which others group and containing seminal concepts of logic, psychology, and metaphysics.

entries.label: The Argument for Justice
entries.summary: The dialogue conducts a search after justice, tracing it from individual impressions through an ideal state, its degeneration, the critique of poetry, and the vision of a future life.

entries.label: Five Natural Divisions
entries.summary: The dialogue can be viewed as five natural divisions, moving from the refutation of common views to the construction of states, philosophical contemplation, perversions of governance, and poetry.

entries.label: Two Opposed Points of View
entries.summary: Alternatively, the work divides into two contrasting halves: a conventional Hellenic state (Books I-IV) and an ideal philosophical kingdom (Books V-X) revealing an imperfect artistic unity.

entries.label: Unity of Justice and the State
entries.summary: Debates over whether justice or statecraft is the principal subject are resolved by showing they are two aspects of the same truth—soul and body, warp and woof.

entries.label: Progression of Morality
entries.summary: The interlocutors—Cephalus, Polemarchus, Thrasymachus, Glaucon, and Adeimantus—represent successive historical and philosophical stages of moral development.

entries.label: Evolution of Socrates
entries.summary: Socrates shifts from an ironical, questioning figure in Book I resembling the historical Socrates to a dogmatic teacher laying out constructive systems and the ideal state.

entries.label: Traditional Moral Precepts
entries.summary: The discussion opens with Cephalus and Polemarchus attempting to define justice as speaking the truth, paying debts, and helping friends while harming enemies, which dialectic finds inadequate.

entries.label: Thrasymachus on Might and Right
entries.summary: Thrasymachus asserts that justice is the interest of the stronger ruler and that supreme injustice is far more profitable and stronger than justice.

entries.label: Analogy of the Arts
entries.summary: Socrates refutes definitions of justice by drawing parallels with the arts, asserting that an art aims at the good of its subjects rather than the artist, and seeks limit rather than excess.

entries.label: Weakness of Evil and Disunity
entries.summary: Socrates argues that evil is inherently discordant and that complete injustice produces absolute weakness, requiring a remnant of justice for even criminals to act together.

entries.label: Justice Desired for Itself
entries.summary: Glaucon and Adeimantus challenge Socrates to prove that justice is desirable in itself apart from external rewards or appearances.

entries.label: Glaucon's Social Compact View
entries.summary: Glaucon frames justice as a compromise and necessity of the weaker to avoid suffering evil, illustrated by the Ring of Gyges and the stripped just man.

entries.label: Adeimantus on External Rewards
entries.summary: Adeimantus points out that parents, poets, and prophets praise justice only for external consequences, reputations, and divine pardons rather than its inherent power in the soul.

entries.label: The Ideal of Justice Apart from Circumstances
entries.summary: The commentator explains that the brothers ask Socrates to demonstrate that justice yields happiness even when stripped of external benefits, defending this method by showing that ideals serve as vital educational and moral benchmarks despite their paradoxical nature compared to everyday human experience.

entries.label: Analogy of State and Individual
entries.summary: Socrates proposes to locate justice by looking first at the larger structure of the city before examining the individual, reflecting early Greek political thought where ethical life is framed through civic community.

entries.label: Genesis of the State and Division of Labour
entries.summary: Society originates from mutual necessity and the satisfaction of basic material needs, requiring specialization where individuals perform functions best aligned with their diverse natural capabilities.

entries.label: The Luxurious City and Origin of Guardians
entries.summary: The transition from the simple rustic community to a luxurious state brings complex arts, resource competition, and war, necessitating a specialized guardian class that must unite spirited courage with philosophical gentleness.

entries.label: Censorship of Theological Narratives
entries.summary: Educational reform requires strict regulation of poetry and myth, decreeing that God must only be depicted as the cause of good and as wholly true and unchanging, to avoid corrupting young citizens with unworthy divine models.

entries.label: The True Lie in the Soul
entries.summary: The commentator examines the distinction between the hateful lie in the soul—an involuntary deception regarding supreme moral and ontological truth—and medicinal verbal fictions regulated for state utility.

entries.label: Restrictions on Poetic Imitation
entries.summary: Guardians are barred from widespread dramatic imitation because assuming unworthy or diverse roles risks reshaping their character, thereby violating the cardinal principle of civic specialization.

entries.label: Purification of Musical Harmony and Rhythm
entries.summary: Musical modes and metres are purged of softness, sorrow, and excessive complexity, preserving only simple Dorian and Phrygian strains that cultivate courageous resilience and temperate self-mastery.

entries.label: Soul and Physical Training
entries.summary: Gymnastics must be kept simple and in service of the soul, avoiding excessive medical coddling and luxury.

entries.label: Harmonizing Reason and Passion
entries.summary: Music and gymnastics are both primarily directed to the soul to achieve harmony between its spirited and philosophic elements.

entries.label: The Myth of the Metals
entries.summary: The state employs the fiction of earthborn men with natures of gold, silver, brass, and iron to legitimate class rank and merit-based transposition.

entries.label: Guardian Communal Discipline
entries.summary: Guardians are denied private property, money, and luxury so that they remain protective watchdogs rather than predatory tyrants.

entries.label: Critique of Platonic Medicine
entries.summary: Commentary notes Plato's failure to appreciate gradual healing, dietetics, and the nuanced interaction of body and mind.

entries.label: Good of the Whole State
entries.summary: In Book IV, Socrates replies to Adeimantus that the objective of the state is the happiness and excellence of the whole, not the exceptional indulgence of any single class.

entries.label: Primacy of Education over Laws
entries.summary: Detailed legislation is useless without proper education, whereas sound education and preservation of musical forms render minute legal enactments unnecessary.

entries.label: Duty Precedes Utility
entries.summary: The commentary evaluates the relation of duty to happiness, arguing that duty and moral right form the true initial foundation of ethics and politics, whereas utilitarian happiness acts as a secondary principle or corrective.

entries.label: Four Cardinal Virtues
entries.summary: Socrates locates wisdom in the guardians, courage in the soldiers, temperance across all classes, and isolates justice by eliminating the other three virtues.

entries.label: Justice as Internal Order
entries.summary: Justice is defined as every class and every element doing its own business, functioning as the comprehensive harmony and health of the state and the soul.

entries.label: Tripartite Soul
entries.summary: Using the principle of contradiction and instances of conflicting impulses, Socrates establishes three distinct principles in the human soul: the rational, the spirited or passionate, and the concupiscent.

entries.label: Equal Roles for Women
entries.summary: Socrates argues that natural differences between men and women do not affect aptitude for governance or warfare, requiring equal education and duties for female guardians.

entries.label: Communal Guardian Family
entries.summary: Guardian marriages, reproduction, and child-rearing are strictly regulated by rulers through rigged lots and common nurseries to remove private domestic ties and maintain civic unity.

entries.label: Civic Unity as Organic Whole
entries.summary: The highest good of a commonwealth is unbroken unity where citizens share pleasures and pains, responding together like a single bodily organism.

entries.label: Philosopher-King Paradox
entries.summary: The ideal city can never become actual until political authority and true philosophy are united in the same persons.

entries.label: Knowledge versus Opinion
entries.summary: Knowledge relates to unchanging real being, ignorance to non-being, and opinion to intermediate contingent objects that both are and are not.

entries.label: Parable of the Ship
entries.summary: An allegory illustrates how mutinous, ignorant sailors disable the true navigator, explaining why authentic philosophers appear useless in contemporary politics.

entries.label: Corruption of Philosophic Nature
entries.summary: Rare gifted natures are easily corrupted by public opinion and social flattery, leaving philosophy abandoned to unworthy pretenders.

entries.label: Idea of the Good
entries.summary: The guardian's higher course of education must culminate in the idea of the good, the supreme principle surpassing wisdom and pleasure.

entries.label: Analogy of the Sun
entries.summary: Socrates introduces the sun as the child of the good, mediating light and sight in the visible realm just as the idea of good mediates truth, being, and knowledge in the intellectual realm.

entries.label: The Divided Line
entries.summary: Socrates divides reality and cognition into four segments, mapping visible shadows and objects to belief and perception, and mathematical hypotheses and dialectical ideas to understanding and reason.

entries.label: Ancient vs Modern Philosopher
entries.summary: The commentator compares the ancient philosophical ideal, aiming toward the idea of the good through unified contemplation, with the modern division of scientific labor and empirical induction.

entries.label: Critique of Plato's Logic
entries.summary: The commentary notes that Plato's dialectic conceives of an ideal self-supporting system of universal knowledge while prematurely attempting to anticipate actual sciences without empirical analysis.

entries.label: Allegory of the Cave
entries.summary: Book VII presents the allegory of chained denizens mistaking cast shadows for reality, whose eventual ascent to the sun represents the painful conversion of the soul toward truth and the good.

entries.label: Compelled Descent of Rulers
entries.summary: Educated philosophers who have perceived the good must be required to return to the underground den to govern, ensuring rule by those least desirous of political ambition.

entries.label: Number as Conductor to Being
entries.summary: Arithmetic and calculation are introduced as the primary disciplines that draw the mind from becoming to being by presenting sensible contradictions that require abstract reflection.

entries.label: Curriculum of Solids and Motion
entries.summary: Socrates arranges the mathematical disciplines in order: plane geometry, solid geometry, astronomy, and harmonics, emphasizing their value for the idea of the good rather than mere practical utility.

entries.label: Dialectic as Coping-Stone
entries.summary: Dialectic is described as the science of absolute truth that dispenses with hypotheses, leading the intellect to the idea of the good as the coping-stone of all sciences.

entries.label: Selection and Lifespan Scheme
entries.summary: Rulers must possess diligence and ability, proceeding from playful study in youth through fragmented sciences, five years of dialectic at thirty, fifteen years in the den, and culmination at fifty.

entries.label: Peril of the Supposititious Son
entries.summary: Premature exposure to dialectical questioning is likened to a supposititious son who loses respect for his reputed parents, causing young students to discard morality and doubt all solid principles.

entries.label: Two Aims of Platonic Thought
entries.summary: The commentary identifies Plato's twin aims as realizing abstractions and connecting them, noting that mathematics aids the mind in drawing away from sense despite potential detachment from facts.

entries.label: Dual Disorders of Eyesight
entries.summary: The political allegory of the cave is illustrated through two kinds of disordered eyesight: theorists blinded by broad abstractions when facing practical affairs, and practical men blinded when confronted with universal principles.

entries.label: Four Degenerate States and Men
entries.summary: Socrates resumes his argument by positing four inferior constitutions—timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny—each corresponding to an individual human character type, to assess relative happiness and misery against the just State.

entries.label: Origin and Nature of Timocracy
entries.summary: Timocracy arises from internal division and unpropitious generation, creating a military-dominated state valuing honor, private property, and war over philosophy, mirrored in an ambitious man torn between an unworldly father and social ambition.

entries.label: Oligarchy and the Divided City
entries.summary: Oligarchy is established when wealth determines political privilege, creating two antagonistic factions of rich and poor, fostering useless drones, and shaping an uneducated man driven solely by avarice and penny-pinching calculation.

entries.label: Democracy and Lawless Freedom
entries.summary: Democracy emerges from the rebellion of the impoverished against oligarchy, resulting in total liberty, disregard for qualifications, and an individual whose soul treats all necessary and unnecessary desires as equal.

entries.label: Tyranny from Excess Liberty
entries.summary: Excessive liberty leads directly to extreme servitude as a popular protector turns into a tyrannical wolf, surrounding himself with mercenaries and preying upon the populace and temples to maintain absolute power.

entries.label: Order of Thought vs History
entries.summary: The editorial commentary argues that Plato's succession of regimes reflects an order of philosophical thought rather than actual historical development in Greek cities.

entries.label: Ethical Gradation of Declines
entries.summary: The commentator notes that each successive constitution reflects an ethical degradation, falling from the rule of reason to honor, then wealth, followed by unrestrained liberty, and finally a single tyrannical monster passion.

entries.label: The Platonic Number of Births
entries.summary: Analysis of the mathematical problem in Book VIII, identifying the number 216 as the cycle of human generations and examining its Pythagorean proportions and harmonies.

entries.label: Genesis of the Tyrant
entries.summary: The progression of the tyrannical soul from lawless nocturnal appetites into dominant passion, madness, and widespread injustice.

entries.label: Misery of the Tyrant
entries.summary: Demonstration that the tyrannical man, especially when ruling a public tyranny, is entirely enslaved, terrified, and the most miserable of individuals.

entries.label: Hierarchy of Pleasures
entries.summary: Evaluation of the three forms of pleasure belonging to reason, passion, and appetite, judged through the superior experience and reason of the philosopher.

entries.label: Interval of King and Tyrant
entries.summary: Calculation placing the happiness of the royal man 729 times above that of the tyrant, using the formula of a cubed relation.

entries.label: Tripartite Image of the Soul
entries.summary: The allegorical figure of the soul combining a many-headed beast, a lion, and an inner human figure under human form to distinguish justice from injustice.

entries.label: The Heavenly Pattern
entries.summary: The concept of an ideal city existing as a celestial pattern according to which an individual orders their own internal life, irrespective of earthly existence.

entries.label: Interval of King and Tyrant
entries.summary: Plato employs the number 729 (the cube of 9) to designate the vast interval separating royal and tyrannical pleasure, treating it as an arithmetical and geometrical representation of an immeasurable difference.

entries.label: Contextualizing Plato on Poetry
entries.summary: The commentator suggests Plato's anti-poetic stance stemmed from contemporary theatrical and political decay, while arguing against Plato that art can express ideal truths beyond mere literal imitation.

entries.label: Plato's Critique of Poetry
entries.summary: Plato objects to poetry and the imitative arts because they indulge emotional and inferior faculties instead of rational abstraction and universals.

entries.label: Higher Function of Art
entries.summary: Art and poetry can mediate between sense and ideas, harmonize feeling with reason, and express divine perfection and moral truth.

entries.label: Cosmology and the Myth of Er
entries.summary: The Vision of Er merges astronomical models with mythological symbolism, using the spindle of Necessity to represent celestial motions.

entries.label: Moral Choice within Necessity
entries.summary: Despite the constraints of destiny and the lot, man retains the freedom of the will to choose a good life if guided by philosophical wisdom rather than mere unreflective habit.

entries.label: The Republic's Dual Nature
entries.summary: The Republic presents two distinct aspects: an Hellenic state rooted in Dorian and Spartan customs, and an ideal philosophical kingdom.

entries.label: Pythagorean League Influence
entries.summary: Plato's Republic incorporates Pythagorean precedents of an aristocracy of virtue, mathematical education, and a shared ascetic rule of life.

entries.label: Ideal State as Vision, Not Fact
entries.summary: Plato's ideal state attempts an impossible union of historical Hellenic institutions with philosophical ideals, functioning as a pattern rather than an earthly reality.

entries.label: Plato's Citizenship and Ideal State
entries.summary: The commentator dismisses Niebuhr's query on Plato's citizenship, explaining that Plato judged all existing polities as states of faction and framed an ideal State transcending particular countries and times.

entries.label: First Paradox: Community of Goods
entries.summary: Introduces the paradox of common property, noting Aristotle's economic criticisms while observing that notions of property were far less fixed and sacred in antiquity and early Christianity than in modern conservatism.

entries.label: Contingency of Property Rights
entries.summary: Argues that private property rests on expediency and may evolve through human progress into more collective forms dedicated to universal culture and public benefit.

entries.label: Equality of Training for Sexes
entries.summary: Details Plato's proposal that women share the education, gymnastics, and civic offices of men, arguing from animal analogies that differences in pursuits are matters of custom rather than essential nature.

entries.label: Second Paradox: Community of Wives
entries.summary: Introduces Plato's radical proposal to dissolve the private family and regulate mating exclusively for the racial improvement of the state.

entries.label: Critique of Platonic Animal Breeding
entries.summary: Rejects Plato's breeding scheme for reducing human beings to brute beasts, neglecting the spiritual and imaginative ties of genuine marriage and Christian recognition of individual value.

entries.label: Futility of Artificial Selection
entries.summary: Contends that human genius and character are too complex to be manufactured through breeding lots, citing historical evidence that great individuals rarely inherit their gifts from notable parents.

entries.label: Limits of Heredity and Will
entries.summary: Heredity transmits mental and physical traits, but it remains immeasurable and leaves room for prevention, cure, and human will.

entries.label: Necessity of the Family Unit
entries.summary: Nature rebukes Plato's foundling system because infants cannot thrive without the irreplaceable sympathy and care of the family.

entries.label: Spartan Model and Individuality
entries.summary: Plato misjudged Sparta, which suppressed individual genius and culture in favour of an unyielding state machine.

entries.label: The Philosopher-Statesman
entries.summary: The philosopher-king ideal faces practical distrust and distortion, yet the synthesis of speculative thought and decisive action remains essential.

entries.label: State-Individual Analogy
entries.summary: Plato fallaciously equates the state to a single individual, conflating politics with ethics, though the comparison still ennobles political ideals.

entries.label: Education for Life and Soul
entries.summary: Education spans the whole of life, aiming not to insert knowledge from without, but to turn the soul toward truth and goodness.

entries.label: Music, Gymnastic, and Character
entries.summary: Early education unites music and gymnastic, using simple harmonious forms and physical discipline to nurture and strengthen the mind.

entries.label: Medicine and Law Simplicity
entries.summary: Plato parallels medicine with law, arguing that both benefit from simplicity and prevention rather than complicated cures and multiplying regulations.

entries.label: Dialectic and Idea of Good
entries.summary: Education advances beyond mathematics to dialectic, which aims at the idea of good—an inspiring yet abstract vision uniting knowledge and reality.

entries.label: Lifelong Self-Education
entries.summary: Plato's vision of continuing education throughout life is praised as an inspiring ideal, though modern application depends on individual self-education.

entries.label: Absence of Progress Idea
entries.summary: Ancient thinkers like Plato and Aristotle lacked the modern idea of progress, conceiving history instead as cyclical destructions and reconstructions governed by fate and chance.

entries.label: Comparison: Republic and Laws
entries.summary: The Republic reflects Plato's hopeful middle period and focuses on an ideal constitution, while the Laws expresses the disillusionment and practical legalism of his old age.

entries.label: Statesman on Law and Rule
entries.summary: The Statesman blends political inquiry with method and dialectic, weighing the rule of law against personal governance while exploring myths of primitive innocence.

entries.label: Cicero's De Republica
entries.summary: Cicero's De Republica adapts Platonic political themes and myths to a Roman oratorical context, though it remains rhetorically clumsy and unoriginal compared to Plato.

entries.label: Cicero's Imitations of Plato
entries.summary: Cicero adapts Platonic concepts such as the vision of Er in the Somnium Scipionis and grounds his ideal state in Roman history, but his rhetorical style and unoriginal philosophy fall short of Plato's art.

entries.label: Augustine's De Civitate Dei
entries.summary: Prompted by the sack of Rome, Augustine develops the ideal of a heavenly city while polemically contrasting pagan corruption with Christian truth, exhibiting deep Christian ethics but an uncritical use of classical sources.

entries.label: Dante's Universal Empire
entries.summary: Dante's De Monarchia champions the necessity of a universal empire possessing divine legitimacy separate from the Papacy to establish earthly peace and freedom.

entries.label: More's Utopia and Platonism
entries.summary: More draws heavily on Platonic ideals, adopting community of property, profound religious tolerance, and sharp social criticism to imagine a just commonwealth against contemporary European decay.

entries.label: Campanella's City of the Sun
entries.summary: Campanella's City of the Sun depicts an ideal state structured around communal property and families, natural scientific education, and public duty to alleviate social ignorance and misery.

entries.label: The Function of Ideals
entries.summary: Ideals lift human conduct above daily routine and commercial self-interest, acting as elevated visions of unrealized perfection rather than immediate practical guides.

entries.label: Modern Dual Ideals and Faith
entries.summary: Modern thought centers on two great ideals: the future progress of humanity in this world and the eternal future of the individual, both harmonized when surrendered to divine will.

entries.label: The Divine Man and the Good
entries.summary: The Christian ideal of the Divine Man unites divine and human nature within the human heart, fulfilling the enduring aspiration toward the Platonic Idea of Good.

entries.label: Old Age and Character
entries.summary: Cephalus explains that old age brings freedom from unruly passions, attributing happiness or misery in later years primarily to personal character rather than age itself.

entries.label: Value of Riches in Age
entries.summary: Cephalus argues that wealth's chief advantage for a good man is relieving the dread of entering the afterlife having deceived others or unpaid debts.

entries.label: Paying Debts Counterexample
entries.summary: Socrates argues that justice cannot simply mean speaking the truth and returning debts, citing the counterexample of withholding weapons from a friend who has become mad.

entries.label: Good to Friends, Harm to Foes
entries.summary: Polemarchus adopts Simonides's view by defining justice as giving what is proper, interpreted as doing good to one's friends and evil to one's enemies.

entries.label: Justice Never Harms
entries.summary: Socrates argues that harming someone deteriorates their virtue and causes injustice, concluding that injuring anyone cannot be the function of a just person.

entries.label: Interest of the Stronger
entries.summary: Thrasymachus asserts that justice is nothing other than the interest of the stronger, manifested in the laws established by rulers for their own benefit.

entries.label: Fallibility of Rulers
entries.summary: Socrates challenges Thrasymachus by showing that rulers can make mistakes regarding their own interests, meaning obeying them could lead to their injury.

entries.label: The unerring ruler qua ruler
entries.summary: Thrasymachus defines a skilled artist or ruler in the strict sense as unerring while exercising that role, claiming the ruler always commands what serves their own interest.

entries.label: Arts serve their subjects
entries.summary: Socrates argues through examples like medicine and piloting that true arts have no defects of their own and look only to the interest and benefit of their weaker subjects.

entries.label: Injustice as wisdom and virtue
entries.summary: Thrasymachus asserts that injustice, especially tyranny on a grand scale, is strong, wise, and profitable, whereas justice is mere simple-mindedness serving another's good.

entries.label: The craftsman does not overreach
entries.summary: Socrates shows that the knowing artist does not seek to exceed or outdo another skilled practitioner in the same art, concluding that the just man resembles the wise and good while the unjust resembles the ignorant.

entries.label: Injustice undermines unity
entries.summary: Socrates argues that injustice creates hatred, division, and inability to act together in states, gangs, or individuals, whereas justice produces harmony.

entries.label: Function and soul's excellence
entries.summary: Socrates establishes that every thing has a specific function (end) and a corresponding virtue (excellence) without which it cannot perform its proper work, applying this to the soul's governance and life.

entries.label: Justice as Excellence of Soul
entries.summary: Justice is acknowledged as the excellence of the soul, while injustice is its defect.

entries.label: Just Soul Lives Well and Happy
entries.summary: Because the just soul lives well, the just person is blessed and happy, whereas the unjust person is miserable.

entries.label: Superior Profit of Justice
entries.summary: Since happiness is profitable and misery is not, injustice can never be more profitable than justice.

entries.label: Editorial Note on Socrates
entries.summary: An editorial sidenote records that Socrates is displeased with himself and with the argument.

entries.label: Socrates' Aporia and Self-Blame
entries.summary: Socrates blames himself for wandering into downstream questions before defining the nature of justice, concluding that he knows nothing.

entries.label: Threefold Division of Goods
entries.summary: Glaucon classifies goods into three kinds: those welcomed for their own sake, those desired both for themselves and their results, and burdensome goods desired only for rewards.

entries.label: Social Contract Origin of Justice
entries.summary: Glaucon articulates the common view that justice is an agreed compromise between the natural good of committing injustice without penalty and the evil of suffering injustice without redress.

entries.label: Ring of Gyges Thought Experiment
entries.summary: Glaucon recounts the tale of Gyges using an invisibility ring to seize power, arguing that anyone freed from fear of discovery would act unjustly.

entries.label: Praise of Justice for External Gain
entries.summary: Adeimantus argues that parents, poets, and prose writers praise justice merely for reputation, social advancement, and divine favour, rather than its intrinsic worth.

entries.label: The Demand to Defend Justice Itself
entries.summary: Adeimantus challenges Socrates to demonstrate what justice and injustice accomplish on their own inside the soul, stripped of external reputations and rewards.

entries.label: State Analogy: The Large Letters
entries.summary: Socrates proposes to locate justice by examining a State first, likening it to reading large letters before examining smaller ones in the individual.

entries.label: Foundation of the State on Human Need
entries.summary: Socrates states that a city originates because individuals are not self-sufficing but have numerous bodily and material needs that require mutual cooperation.

entries.label: Specialization and Division of Labour
entries.summary: Socrates and Adeimantus deduce that work is better and more plentiful when each citizen performs the single craft fitted to their natural disposition.

entries.label: The Luxurious State and War
entries.summary: When Glaucon seeks comforts beyond the simple city, Socrates introduces the luxurious State; its need for unlimited wealth requires seizing neighbors' territory, making war inevitable.

entries.label: Specialization of the Guardian
entries.summary: Because one person cannot master multiple arts, war requires dedicated practitioners who possess natural aptitudes and undergo continuous training as guardians.

entries.label: Spirited and Philosophical Nature
entries.summary: Guardians must combine spirit with gentleness toward fellow citizens, illustrated by well-bred dogs who distinguish friend from stranger through knowledge.

entries.label: Censorship of Early Stories
entries.summary: Because young minds absorb impressions indelibly, the founders must censor poets and storytellers, rejecting myths of divine conflicts and crimes.

entries.label: God is the Author of Good Only
entries.summary: Since God is good and not hurtful, God cannot cause evil; God is the author of only the good things in human life, not of all things.

entries.label: Divine Immutability and Truthfulness
entries.summary: Being already perfect, God neither alters form nor deceives mortals with lies or phantoms, establishing the second standard for poetry.

entries.label: Censorship of the Underworld
entries.summary: Tales depicting the world below as terrible and lamentable must be expunged so that guardians do not fear death or prefer slavery to dying in battle.

entries.label: Rulers' Privilege of Lying
entries.summary: Truth is strictly valued, meaning private citizens may not lie, whereas rulers alone retain the privilege of using falsehoods like medicine for the public good.

entries.label: Modes of Poetic Narration
entries.summary: Poetic style is divided into simple narrative, pure imitation (as in tragedy and comedy), or a combination of both (as in epic poetry).

entries.label: Restriction of Imitation
entries.summary: Because one person can perform only one role well, guardians must not imitate diverse or base characters, lest imitation become second nature and corrupt their virtue.

entries.label: Exclusion of Pantomimic Poets
entries.summary: The versatile poet who imitates all manners and sounds will be revered as holy but expelled from the city in favor of the austere storyteller who imitates virtue alone.

entries.label: Regulation of Musical Harmonies
entries.summary: Melody must conform to words, requiring the elimination of sorrowful and relaxed harmonies like the Lydian and Ionian, leaving only martial and temperate modes.

entries.label: Retention of Dorian and Phrygian
entries.summary: Socrates restricts acceptable harmonies to two: a warlike strain for crisis and courage, and a peaceful strain for prudence and temperance, identified as the Dorian and Phrygian.

entries.label: Exclusion of Complex Music
entries.summary: Instruments with multiple strings, complex scales, or flute-like versatility are banned from the city to purge luxury, keeping only the lyre, harp, and rustic pipe.

entries.label: Primacy of Simplicity in Style
entries.summary: Rhythm and harmony must follow the words, and the words reflect the soul; therefore, true beauty and grace depend on the simplicity of a well-ordered character.

entries.label: Potency of Musical Education
entries.summary: Musical training is deemed the most potent education because rhythm and harmony sink deep into the soul, imparting grace and instilling intuitive love of the good before rational maturity.

entries.label: Critique of Lingering Medicine
entries.summary: Socrates condemns valetudinarian medicine that pampers chronic diseases and prolongs unproductive lives, maintaining that citizens have civic duties and must not spend their lives nursing ailments.

entries.label: Judicial Knowledge Without Evil
entries.summary: Unlike a physician who benefits from bodily experience of disease, a good judge must remain uncorrupted by vice in youth and acquire knowledge of evil late through observation of others.

entries.label: Harmony of Music and Gymnastic
entries.summary: Music and gymnastic are both designed chiefly for the soul to tune and balance the spirited and philosophic elements, preventing ferocity on one side and effeminacy on the other.

entries.label: Selection of Rulers
entries.summary: Socrates establishes that rulers must be drawn from the elder guardians who demonstrate unwavering devotion to the welfare of the city across all stages of life.

entries.label: Testing the Guardians
entries.summary: Candidates are subjected to trials involving deception, fear, toil, and temptation to ensure they never abandon their conviction to prioritize the commonwealth.

entries.label: Separation of Rulers and Auxiliaries
entries.summary: Full guardianship is assigned strictly to the proven elders, while younger warriors are designated as auxiliaries who enforce the rulers' policies.

entries.label: The Myth of the Metals
entries.summary: Socrates proposes a civic narrative asserting that citizens are born from the earth with soul compositions of gold, silver, brass, or iron, which dictates their societal roles while permitting mobility based on natural merit.

entries.label: Communal Living and Prohibition of Property
entries.summary: Auxiliaries and rulers are prohibited from holding private property, money, or individual dwellings to prevent them from becoming predatory tyrants over the citizenry.

entries.label: Adeimantus's Objection
entries.summary: Adeimantus raises the charge that Socrates denies the guardians wealth, land, and ordinary luxuries, effectively making them miserable mercenaries in their own city.

entries.label: Happiness of the Whole State
entries.summary: Socrates argues that the purpose of founding the state is the greatest happiness of the whole rather than any single class, comparing the state to a statue whose parts must be painted proportionally.

entries.label: Primacy of Nurture and Music
entries.summary: Socrates asserts that proper education and strict maintenance of music and gymnastic without innovation preserve civic order and prevent creeping lawlessness.

entries.label: Wisdom and Courage Identified
entries.summary: Socrates locates civic wisdom in the small ruling class possessing knowledge for the whole state, and civic courage in the soldiers whose education preserves the law's conviction regarding what is to be feared.

entries.label: Temperance as Harmony
entries.summary: Temperance is defined not as the property of a single class, but as an agreement and harmony throughout the whole state wherein the naturally worse part is governed by the better.

entries.label: Justice as Doing One's Business
entries.summary: Socrates identifies civic justice as the foundational principle that each citizen must perform the single task for which nature best suited them, minding their own business without meddling in others'.

entries.label: Justice in the State
entries.summary: Justice in the city is identified as the condition wherein each class—trader, auxiliary, and guardian—performs its proper task without meddling in the duties of others.

entries.label: Principle of Non-Contradiction
entries.summary: The same entity cannot act or be acted upon in contrary manners simultaneously within the same part and in relation to the same object.

entries.label: Tripartite Soul
entries.summary: The soul is composed of three distinct principles—rational, spirited, and appetitive—mirrored by conflicting impulses such as Leontius's anger against his desires.

entries.label: Individual Justice as Harmony
entries.summary: Justice in the individual is defined not merely by outward deeds, but by an inner harmony where reason governs, spirit aids, and appetites are contained.

entries.label: Virtue as Soul Health
entries.summary: Virtue and vice in the soul correspond directly to health and disease in the body, rendering the question of whether injustice is profitable absurd.

entries.label: Five Constitutions and Souls
entries.summary: Socrates establishes that there are five distinct forms of the State matching five forms of the soul, beginning with aristocracy/monarchy.

entries.label: Interruption of Book V
entries.summary: Adeimantus and the company halt Socrates' transition to discussing degenerate states, insisting on a thorough account of how women and children are held in common.

entries.label: Equal Duties and Training
entries.summary: Socrates argues from animal analogies that female guardians must participate equally in defense and governance, requiring identical education in music, gymnastics, and war.

entries.label: Difference of Nature Clarified
entries.summary: Socrates resolves the apparent contradiction regarding specialization by distinguishing between incidental biological differences and differences relevant to civic capacities.

entries.label: Distribution of Natural Gifts
entries.summary: Socrates posits that nature's governing and philosophical talents are distributed across both sexes, even if the female sex is held to be generally weaker.

entries.label: Regulated Mating and Families
entries.summary: Socrates proposes that guardians share spouses and offspring, with state-regulated pairing by rigged lotteries, collective rearing, and collective kinship designations.

entries.label: Civic Unity as Supreme Good
entries.summary: Socrates identifies internal cohesion through shared joy and pain as the greatest civic good, contrasting it with private fragmentation.

entries.label: Unity of the Best-Ordered State
entries.summary: A state achieves optimal order and cohesion when citizens share feelings in common, likening the commonwealth to an individual body where hurt to any single part affects the whole.

entries.label: Inter-Hellenic Conduct and War
entries.summary: Warfare between Hellenic states is categorized as internal discord among natural friends, prohibiting enslavement, corpse-looting, and the devastation of lands.

entries.label: Ideals as Evaluative Standards
entries.summary: An ideal pattern of justice or a perfect state serves as an absolute standard for evaluation and is not rendered invalid merely because it cannot be realized in every concrete detail.

entries.label: The Philosopher-King Paradox
entries.summary: Political evils in cities and humankind will not end until political greatness and wisdom unite through philosophers ruling as kings.

entries.label: Desire for the Whole of Wisdom
entries.summary: Analogous to lovers of youth, wine, and honor who cherish every instance of their object, the philosopher is characterized by a desire for all knowledge and wisdom, not merely a part.

entries.label: Lovers of the Vision of Truth
entries.summary: True philosophers are defined as lovers of the vision of truth, distinguishing them from sight-seers, sound-lovers, and musical amateurs who only imitate the pursuit of knowledge.

entries.label: Unity of Forms and the Many
entries.summary: Socrates establishes that opposing concepts such as beauty and ugliness, or just and unjust, are each individually one, yet appear manifold due to their combination with bodies, actions, and other things.

entries.label: Philosophers versus Dreamers
entries.summary: Lovers of sights and sounds substitute beautiful particulars for absolute beauty, resembling dreamers, whereas true philosophers apprehend absolute beauty itself without confusing it with participating objects.

entries.label: Definition of a Faculty
entries.summary: Faculties are defined as internal powers distinguished not by perceptual features like shape or color, but solely by their distinctive sphere of operation and resultant effect.

entries.label: Knowledge and Opinion as Separate
entries.summary: Because knowledge is infallible and opinion is fallible, they constitute distinct faculties and therefore must relate to distinct subject matters.

entries.label: Opinion as Intermediate Faculty
entries.summary: Since knowledge correlates to what is (being) and ignorance to what is not (not-being), opinion is situated as an intermediate faculty between knowledge and ignorance.

entries.label: Fluctuating Nature of Particulars
entries.summary: Sensory particulars such as beautiful, just, or double things necessarily exhibit their opposite qualities, making them ambiguous entities that both are and are not.

entries.label: Lovers of Opinion vs. Wisdom
entries.summary: Those who delight in the manifold fluctuating particulars hold opinions and are lovers of opinion, while those who embrace unchanging eternal truth are lovers of wisdom.

entries.label: Philosopher as Ideal Guardian
entries.summary: Socrates argues that those who know the eternal, unchanging truth of things with clear vision, while lacking nothing in experience or virtue, are the only fit guardians of the State.

entries.label: Nature of the True Philosopher
entries.summary: The true philosopher possesses an innate love of all true being, detests falsehood, seeks pleasures of the soul over bodily desire, is temperate and brave, and possesses memory, proportion, and quickness of learning.

entries.label: Charge of Roguery and Uselessness
entries.summary: Adeimantus objects that common experience shows dedicated philosophers become useless oddities or utter rogues, rendering the claim that they should rule paradoxical.

entries.label: Parable of the Ship of State
entries.summary: Socrates compares the city to a mutinous vessel where ignorant sailors vie for control of a dull captain and dismiss the true navigator, who studies skies and seasons, as a useless star-gazer.

entries.label: Corruption of Gifted Natures
entries.summary: Finest minds suffer the greatest injury in unsuitable conditions; flattery, societal praise and blame, and worldly advantages divert gifted souls into doing great evil.

entries.label: Usurpation by Unworthy Imitators
entries.summary: When genuine disciples desert philosophy, base artisans and puny natures occupy the vacuum, producing sophisms rather than genuine wisdom.

entries.label: The Sheltered Remnant
entries.summary: The small band of true philosophers, unable to alter the madness of the multitude and lacking an aligned state, must shelter under a wall and live quietly without participating in civic life.

entries.label: Alienation from Existing States
entries.summary: No current constitution suits the philosophical nature, leaving it to degenerate like an exotic seed unless a state matching its own perfection is established.

entries.label: Education in Philosophy
entries.summary: Socrates criticizes the prevailing superficial and premature study of philosophy, arguing instead for a curriculum that pairs youth with bodily training and reserves intensive dialectical study and retirement for mature years.

entries.label: Philosopher-Ruler Feasibility
entries.summary: Socrates argues that establishing an ideal constitution is difficult but not impossible, provided at least one philosopher comes to power and drafts laws by gazing upon absolute virtues.

entries.label: Reconciliation with Multitude
entries.summary: Socrates maintains that the multitude will cease their hostility toward philosophy if they are shown true philosophers, who contemplate unchanging divine order rather than engaging in petty quarrels.

entries.label: Supremacy of the Idea of Good
entries.summary: Socrates asserts that the idea of the good is the highest knowledge, without which all other knowledge and virtues lack utility and true value.

entries.label: Analogy of the Sun
entries.summary: Socrates uses the sun as an offspring of the good, explaining that just as the sun illuminates the visible world and enables sight, the good illuminates the intelligible realm and causes truth and knowledge.

entries.label: The Divided Line
entries.summary: Socrates divides reality into visible and intelligible spheres, using a proportioned line to distinguish shadows and sensible objects from mathematical hypotheses and higher dialectical insight.

entries.label: Dialectical ascent and descent
entries.summary: Reason uses hypotheses as points of departure to ascend to the first principle of the whole, and then descends purely through ideas without sensible aids.

entries.label: Dialectic vs arts' hypotheses
entries.summary: The interlocutor restates that dialectic contemplates clearer knowledge than the arts (like geometry), which proceed from hypotheses without ascending to a first principle.

entries.label: Four faculties of the soul
entries.summary: Four faculties—reason, understanding, faith, and perception of shadows—are aligned with the four divisions, possessing clearness proportional to the truth of their objects.

entries.label: Assent to the fourfold schema
entries.summary: The interlocutor understands, assents to, and accepts the proposed arrangement of the faculties.

entries.label: Allegory of the Cave
entries.summary: Socrates describes human beings chained from childhood in an underground den, seeing only shadows projected by firelight on a wall and mistaking them for true realities.

entries.label: The Ascent to the Sun
entries.summary: When dragged into the upper world, a prisoner is initially dazzled, gradually grows accustomed to reflections and nocturnal celestial bodies, and ultimately contemplates the sun as the cause of all things visible.

entries.label: Ascent of the Soul to Good
entries.summary: Socrates decodes the allegory: the cave is the visible realm, the sun is the Idea of the Good, and the ascent represents the soul's arduous journey into the intellectual world.

entries.label: Turning the Soul's Eye
entries.summary: Education is not putting knowledge into a soul lacking it, but the conversion and turning round of the whole soul's existing organ of vision from the realm of becoming to that of being.

entries.label: Philosophers Must Rule
entries.summary: Philosophers who have attained contemplation of the Good must be compelled to descend back into the cave to govern, ensuring the welfare of the whole commonwealth rather than their own private bliss.

entries.label: Arithmetic as Soul-Turner
entries.summary: Arithmetic and calculation draw the soul toward true being because sensible perceptions of unity evoke contradictions (the one and the many), compelling pure intellect to resolve them.

entries.label: Geometry Directed to Being
entries.summary: While geometry has practical military uses, its true higher philosophical aim is knowledge of the eternal, making the vision of the idea of good easier by compelling the soul toward being.

entries.label: Solid Geometry Curriculum
entries.summary: Socrates corrects the order of instruction, explaining that three-dimensional geometry of solids in themselves must precede the study of solids in motion.

entries.label: Abstract Astronomy and Harmonics
entries.summary: True astronomy and harmonics must leave visible skies and audible sounds behind, utilizing mathematical and rational problems instead of empirical observation.

entries.label: Dialectic as Coping-Stone
entries.summary: Dialectic is established as the supreme science that discards hypotheses to ascend directly to pure being and the essential nature of the good through reason alone.

entries.label: Curricular Ages and Service
entries.summary: Socrates details the progressive stages of testing and training: unforced preliminary studies in youth, physical training, integration at twenty, dialectic at thirty, fifteen years of public office, and ultimate contemplation at fifty.

entries.label: Danger of Premature Dialectic
entries.summary: Using the analogy of a supposititious son, Socrates shows how youthful exposure to dialectic can lead to lawlessness and skepticism when traditional moral codes are refuted.

entries.label: Founding of the Ideal State
entries.summary: Socrates proposes that philosopher-kings will found the just city most readily by sending away everyone over ten and educating the young in new laws.

entries.label: Four Imperfect Constitutions
entries.summary: Socrates resumes the project of comparing four principal inferior constitutions—Cretan/Spartan (timocracy), oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny—and their matching human characters to determine the relative happiness of justice versus injustice.

entries.label: State-Soul Correspondence
entries.summary: Governments mirror the dispositions of the individuals within them, as states arise not from 'oak and rock' but from human characters.

entries.label: Fall of the Ideal State
entries.summary: Due to sensory limitation, rulers miscalculate the geometrical number regulating births, leading to inferior progeny, the corruption of guardians, neglect of music, mixing of metals, and factional partition of common property into private land.

entries.label: The Timocratic Character
entries.summary: Dominated by the spirited element, the timocrat is ambitious, contentious, fond of war and physical culture, and torn between his easy-going father and complaints from his mother and servants.

entries.label: Definition of Oligarchy
entries.summary: Oligarchy is defined as a regime founded on property valuation where the rich hold power and the poor are excluded, splitting the city into two hostile camps.

entries.label: The Drone Analogy
entries.summary: Unchecked accumulation and dispossession generate a class of non-productive citizens likened to drones in a hive—some stingless (paupers) and others possessing stings (criminals).

entries.label: The Oligarchical Character
entries.summary: Witnessing the ruin of his timocratic father, the oligarchical youth dethrones spirit and ambition to enthrone avarice, subduing all unnecessary desires through fear and compulsion.

entries.label: Transition to Democracy
entries.summary: The insatiable desire for riches in an oligarchy drives usury, ruins men of position, and fills the city with armed, disenfranchised paupers who discover the physical weakness and idleness of their rulers.

entries.label: Nature and Rise of Democracy
entries.summary: Democracy originates when the impoverished populace revolts against and expels or executes their wealthy rulers, instituting equal power, shared freedom, and offices assigned by lot.

entries.label: Democratic Freedom and Diversity
entries.summary: Democratic governance prioritizes unchecked individual liberty and speech, producing a state with every variety of human character and assorted constitutions.

entries.label: Division of Desires
entries.summary: Pleasures and desires are bifurcated into necessary desires, which are beneficial and essential to life, and unnecessary desires, which are dispensable, costly, and injurious to virtue.

entries.label: The Democratic Individual
entries.summary: The democratic character emerges from an oligarchic upbringing as unnecessary desires overcome restraint, leading to a life governed by shifting whims, lack of hierarchy, and indiscriminate indulgence.

entries.label: Excessive Liberty Breeds Tyranny
entries.summary: An insatiable thirst for freedom dissolves all forms of social and legal restraint, causing an extreme reaction where absolute liberty transforms into extreme subjugation.

entries.label: Three Classes in a Democracy
entries.summary: Democracies comprise three groups: parasitic spendthrifts and demagogues, the orderly and wealthy class that is despoiled, and the working masses who follow those who provide distributions.

entries.label: The Protector's Metamorphosis
entries.summary: Emerging as a champion of the multitude against the wealthy, the demagogue sheds citizen blood through trumped-up charges, demands a personal bodyguard, and eventually rules as a complete tyrant.

entries.label: The Tyrant's Rule and Parricide
entries.summary: To maintain power, the tyrant instigates continual warfare, purges capable and virtuous citizens, hires mercenary guards, and violently subjugates the very citizenry that empowered him.

entries.label: Genesis of the Tyrannical Man
entries.summary: Socrates describes how lawless appetites, normally restrained or exposed only during dreams, take over when a master passion establishes tyrannical rule over a person's soul.

entries.label: The Private vs. Public Tyrant
entries.summary: Socrates argues that while a private tyrannical person is miserable, one who becomes a public ruler is cast into extreme danger, suspicion, and complete servitude to fear.

entries.label: First Proof: Virtue and Happiness
entries.summary: Socrates proclaims the first proof: the most royal and just individual is the happiest, whereas the most unjust and tyrannical is the most miserable.

entries.label: The Tripartite Soul and Pleasures
entries.summary: The soul is divided into three components—appetitive, spirited, and rational—each pursuing its own corresponding desire and pleasure: gain, honor, and truth.

entries.label: Philosopher's Judgment on Pleasure
entries.summary: Because the philosopher possesses experience of all three pleasures as well as wisdom and reason, his assessment placing intellectual pleasure first is uniquely valid.

entries.label: The Intermediate State of Rest
entries.summary: Socrates identifies an intermediate state of rest between pleasure and pain, demonstrating that relief from pain is an illusory relative pleasure rather than genuine, positive pleasure.

entries.label: Pleasures of Smell Example
entries.summary: The sensation of scent is provided as an instance of pure pleasure that arises without prior suffering or deficit and departs without pain.

entries.label: True vs Illusory Pleasure
entries.summary: Pleasures derived from filling the soul with invariable truth and essence are more real than bodily satisfactions, which are mixed with pain and mistaken for positive pleasure.

entries.label: The 729-Fold Interval
entries.summary: Socrates calculates by cubing distances that a king lives 729 times more pleasantly than a tyrant, who is furthest removed from law and reason.

entries.label: The Composite Soul Image
entries.summary: Socrates models the soul as a composite creature consisting of a multiform beast, a lion, and an inner man, enclosed within a human outward form.

entries.label: Refutation of Injustice
entries.summary: Praising injustice is shown to mean feeding the insatiable monster and starving the inner man, whereas justice subjects the lower beasts to divine reason.

entries.label: Subjection to Divine Rule
entries.summary: It is best for every person to be governed by divine wisdom within, or alternatively by external law, as demonstrated by the rearing of children.

entries.label: Internal City Pattern
entries.summary: The wise person governs bodily desires and wealth to maintain internal harmony, living according to the ideal heavenly city regardless of earthly existence.

entries.label: Rejection of Imitative Poetry
entries.summary: Socrates affirms that imitative poetry must be excluded from the ideal commonwealth, arguing that knowledge of its true character is the sole remedy against its harmful effects.

entries.label: The Three Beds and Makers
entries.summary: Socrates illustrates the hierarchy of reality using three levels of beds: the ideal form made by God, the physical bed fashioned by the craftsman, and the painter's two-dimensional appearance.

entries.label: The Imitator as Thrice Removed
entries.summary: Socrates argues that mimetic artists, including tragic poets like Homer, create only appearances of appearances without genuine knowledge of reality or craft.

entries.label: Using, Making, and Imitating
entries.summary: Socrates distinguishes three relations to any instrument: the user who possesses knowledge, the maker who gains right belief from the user, and the imitator who possesses neither.

entries.label: Appeal to the Inferior Soul
entries.summary: Imitation appeals to the emotionally volatile, unmeasured part of the soul rather than the rational and calculating element, undermining inner moral order.

entries.label: The Ancient Quarrel
entries.summary: Socrates notes the longstanding conflict between philosophy and poetry, permitting poetry's return only if its defenders can prove its moral and political usefulness.

entries.label: Immortality of the Soul
entries.summary: Socrates turns the conversation from earthly virtue to its eternal significance, proposing to an astonished Glaucon that the human soul is immortal and imperishable.

entries.label: Soul's Immortality via Evil
entries.summary: Things are destroyed only by their specific inherent evils; since moral vice does not consume or destroy the soul, and external bodily ailments cannot destroy it directly, the soul is indestructible and immortal.

entries.label: The Soul in Original Purity
entries.summary: The soul's present condition is compared to the encrusted sea-god Glaucus; its genuine nature is revealed only when viewed in purity through its love of wisdom and kinship with the divine.

entries.label: Restoration of Virtue's Rewards
entries.summary: Having established that justice is inherently good for the soul without external incentives, Socrates reintroduces the reputation, honors, and divine protections that the just receive from gods and men in life.

entries.label: Posthumous Judgement of Er
entries.summary: Socrates narrates the journey of Er, recounting the post-mortem judgement of souls, tenfold retributions or rewards for deeds, and the terrifying eternal fate of incurable tyrants like Ardiaeus.

entries.label: Cosmic Spindle of Necessity
entries.summary: Souls witness the cosmic structure turned by the spindle of Necessity, governed by eight rotating concentric whorls, the sirens' harmonies, and the three Fates who guide past, present, and future.

entries.label: The Soul's Choice of Destiny
entries.summary: Souls are offered lots to select their next lives under the rule that virtue is free and choice rests with the chooser; those lacking philosophy often choose poorly, blinded by past habit.

entries.label: Rebirth and Final Exhortation
entries.summary: After drinking from the river of Unmindfulness and being propelled into rebirth, the preserved tale grounds Socrates' final plea to practice justice and virtue always.

entries.label: Plato's Conception of Art
entries.summary: The editorial commentary outlines Plato's evaluation of art through the standard of simplicity, moderation, and censorship, balancing aesthetic influence against the threat of unmanliness.

entries.label: Communism and State Unity
entries.summary: The editor analyzes Plato's abolition of private possession and family in the ideal state as an effort to eliminate division, noting adjustments between the Republic, Critias, and Laws.

entries.label: Dialectic versus Eristic
entries.summary: Dialectic is characterized as the coping stone of the sciences that uses hypotheses to ascend to ideas, distinguished sharply from contentious disputation (eristic).

entries.label: Two Tiers of Education
entries.summary: The editorial apparatus outlines the dual educational curriculum: common training in gymnastics and music for citizens, followed by advanced mathematical and dialectical training for rulers.

entries.label: Platonic Theology
entries.summary: Editorial note summarizing Plato's theology under two heads: God is perfect and unchangeable, and God is true and the author of truth, which serves as a canon to judge poetry.

entries.label: Succession of Constitutions
entries.summary: Editorial analysis of Plato's classification of governments, linking the descent from aristocracy to timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny to the divisions of the soul.

entries.label: Qualifications of Guardians
entries.summary: Index entry documenting the requirements for guardians, including philosophical wisdom, spirited and gentle nature, community of goods, and tests of pleasure and pain.

entries.label: Critique of Homer and Poetry
entries.summary: Index entry citing Plato's critique of Homer and mimetic poetry as thrice removed from the truth, unsuitable for moral education, and portraying gods falsely.

entries.label: Idea of the Good
entries.summary: Editorial note framing the Idea of the Good as an abstraction of perfection uniting beauty, symmetry, and truth, and the source of truth and being.

entries.label: Nature and Role of Justice
entries.summary: Editorial analysis identifying justice as the foundational inquiry of the Republic, defined politically as each person doing their own work and internally as psychic harmony.

entries.label: Ancient Music and Education
entries.summary: The editor details how music among the ancients encompassed mental culture and preparatory education before gymnastic training, highlighting Plato's curriculum across the Republic and Laws.

entries.label: Index: The Philosopher
entries.summary: An extensive index entry outlining citations across the Republic regarding the qualities, hazards, corruptions, and ruling duties of the philosopher.

entries.label: Critique of Poetry
entries.summary: An editorial essay tracing Plato's examination of poetry's educational and cultural role, culminating in the demand for censorship or expulsion in the ideal commonwealth.

entries.label: Index: The Ruler
entries.summary: An index entry indexing references on the testing, qualification, and philosopher-king duties of rulers in the ideal republic.

entries.label: Platonic Psychology
entries.summary: An editorial discussion examining the Republic's tripartite soul, the four intellectual faculties, and the arguments and myths surrounding the soul's immortality and transmigration.

entries.label: Index: The State
entries.summary: An index list referencing the development, social classes, governance, corruptions, and unity of the state in the Republic.

entries.label: Dual Composition of State
entries.summary: An editorial note analyzes the Republic's state as a composite of an older Spartan/Athenian Hellenic model and an ideal commonwealth governed by philosopher-rulers sharing common property.

entries.label: Spartan and Athenian Elements
entries.summary: The state borrows its small civic scale, subordination of the individual, warrior focus, and common meals from Sparta, while drawing its intellectual culture and ruling discipline from Athens.

entries.label: Peculiar Ideal Innovations
entries.summary: Plato's most distinctive concepts—communal property, the equal social and military station of women, and the rule of philosophers—had few real-world precedents in Greek antiquity.

entries.label: Index Entries: Nature of Virtue
entries.summary: The apparatus catalogues instances where virtue is discussed as the health and harmony of the soul, divided into distinct parts, and contrasted with bodily care and wealth.

entries.label: Transcriber Editorial Notes
entries.summary: Editorial notes provide documentation of typographic corrections, collation details, and the structural markup used for marginal Stephanus numbers and Greek transliteration.

entries.label: Front Matter and Revision Notes
entries.summary: Jowett presents the third edition of the translation with extensive alterations affecting roughly one-third of the text, accompanied by dedications, contributor acknowledgments, an exchange plan for previous owners, and plans for future dialogue publications.

entries.label: Structural and Dialectic Evolution
entries.summary: Commentary outlines the five natural structural movements of the Republic, tracing how the interlocutors represent developing stages of morality and how Socrates evolves from an ironical inquirer into a constructive teacher.

entries.label: Book I Notions of Justice
entries.summary: Discussions analyze early definitions of justice, including Cephalus's perspective on wealth alleviating fear of divine retribution and Socrates's examination and subsequent displeasure with the conversational outcome.

entries.label: Pythagorean and Cosmic Motifs
entries.summary: Analyses explore Platonic cosmology and metaphysics, highlighting the calculation of the cyclical number of births, the celestial mechanics of the Myth of Er, and the institutional influences of the Pythagorean league.

entries.label: Comparative Political Ideals
entries.summary: The commentary surveys related political works, comparing Plato's Statesman, Cicero's De Republica, and Dante's vision of universal empire against Platonic philosophical governance.

entries.label: Philosophical and Civic Ideals
entries.summary: Commentaries examine the broad metaphysical and architectural design of the Republic, emphasizing its dual structure balancing a traditional Hellenic polity against an ideal philosophical commonwealth, alongside allegories contrasting theoretical contemplation with practical civic affairs.

entries.label: Book I Debates on Justice
entries.summary: Book I dialogue traverses early conceptions of justice: Cephalus discusses character and passions in old age, Socrates refutes returning debts to the mad and tests ruler fallibility, Polemarchus defines justice as helping friends and harming foes, Thrasymachus praises injustice as profitable power, and Socrates affirms justice as the soul's excellence.

entries.label: The Intrinsic Value of Justice
entries.summary: Glaucon and Adeimantus, echoed across Book II dialogues and introductory summaries, challenge Socrates to demonstrate that justice is desirable entirely in itself, contrasting its inner soul-reality against common praises based on external rewards, reputation, or the impunity demonstrated by the Ring of Gyges.

entries.label: State and Individual Analogy
entries.summary: Socrates introduces the method of examining justice in the larger letters of the State before reading the smaller letters in the individual, establishing the civic framework for the dialogue's moral inquiry.

entries.label: Reception and Utopian Parallels
entries.summary: Commentary examines how Plato's political vision contrasts with his later Laws and inspired subsequent philosophical traditions, including Cicero's historical adaptations, Augustine's heavenly city, More's social critiques, and Campanella's communal state.

entries.label: Communal Guardian Regulations
entries.summary: The guardian class is subjected to strict collective discipline, forbidding private wealth, personal property, and domestic family units in favor of state-regulated unions and common nurseries.

entries.label: Philosopher Education and Dangers
entries.summary: Socrates outlines an ascending mathematical curriculum aimed at eternal reality and a lifespan scheme for dialectic, cautioning against the moral erosion that premature philosophical questioning can trigger.

entries.label: Degeneration of States and Souls
entries.summary: This sequence charts the stepwise decay of regimes and matching soul types from timocracy and oligarchy to chaotic democracy and full-blown tyrannical rule.

entries.label: Mathematical Interval of Happiness
entries.summary: Commentary analyzes the numerical and geometrical formula calculating that the royal ruler experiences 729 times the happiness of the tyrant.

entries.label: Early Education and State Myths
entries.summary: The origins of guardians in a luxurious state require disciplined physical and moral training, encompassing the censorship of theological poetry, constraints on musical modes and imitative drama, simple bodily regimen, and the legitimating myth of earthborn metals.

entries.label: Virtues and Philosopher-Rulers
entries.summary: Civic justice and cardinal virtues establish proper governance, yet authentic philosophers are rejected like true pilots in a mutinous crew; nevertheless, those trained by mathematical abstractions toward true being must be compelled to descend and rule.

entries.label: Justice, Tyranny, and Happiness
entries.summary: Socrates argues that the just soul lives well and achieves true profit and happiness, while the tyrannical ruler represents the extreme opposite, living in utter terror, enslavement, and misery.

entries.label: Critique of Ideal State Reforms
entries.summary: Commentary examines Plato's overarching political vision alongside its radical paradoxes—including the abolition of private property, communal family arrangements, the expulsion of poetry, and the problematic emulation of Spartan collectivism over individual genius.

entries.label: Guardian Natures in Book II
entries.summary: Socrates establishes that the guardian role requires rigorous lifelong specialization and natural aptitude. Candidates must unite spirited courage with philosophical gentleness toward fellow citizens, much like well-bred watchdogs.

entries.label: Censorship of Poetry and Music
entries.summary: Socrates regulates cultural storytelling and artistic expression in Book III to mold guardian character. Reforms include expunging frightening descriptions of Hades, reserving medicinal falsehoods exclusively for rulers, prohibiting harmful poetic imitation, banishing overly versatile or sorrowful harmonies in favor of Dorian and Phrygian modes, and eliminating complex musical instruments.

entries.label: Guardian Trials and Austerity
entries.summary: Guardian candidates undergo exhaustive testing against fear, toil, and seduction to identify true rulers, separating them from auxiliary enforcers. In response, Adeimantus objects that denying rulers property, money, and private luxury renders them unhappy mercenaries in their own commonwealth.

entries.label: Book V Communal Life and Warfare
entries.summary: Interrupted by Adeimantus to clarify communal arrangements, Socrates outlines equal education and military duties for female guardians alongside state-regulated reproduction and common families. He further prescribes restraint during inter-Hellenic warfare, defining conflicts between Greek states as civil discord rather than absolute war.

entries.label: Origin of War and Early Tales
entries.summary: Socrates describes how luxury drives the city into expansion and warfare, and establishes strict regulation of poetic tales to properly shape the impressionable minds of future guardians.

entries.label: Practices of Healing and Law
entries.summary: Socrates critiques protracted medical regimens that distract citizens from civic tasks and contrasts physical healing with the qualifications of a good judge, who must grasp evil by observation rather than personal habit.

entries.label: Foundational Guardian Order
entries.summary: Socrates details the selection of rulers, the myth of the metals, the prohibition of private possessions for guardians, and the civic manifestations of wisdom and courage.

entries.label: Philosophic Capacities & Nature
entries.summary: Socrates outlines how governing aptitudes are distributed across sexes and distinguishes genuine philosophers as those who contemplate ultimate truth rather than superficial appearances.

entries.label: Index: Guardians, Homer, Rulers
entries.summary: The editorial apparatus compiles references detailing the testing and traits of guardians and rulers, as well as citations criticizing Homer and poetic imitation.

entries.label: Index: Virtues, State & Mind
entries.summary: Paratextual entries index passages throughout the work on the definition of virtue, the governance and structural evolution of the state, and the philosopher's development.

entries.label: Commentary on Plato's Polity
entries.summary: The editorial commentary examines historical Spartan and Athenian models influencing Plato's city alongside novel radical proposals like philosopher-rulers and communal living.

entries.label: Foundational Civic Justice
entries.summary: Socrates establishes that civic justice consists in each class minding its own assigned role and outlines five corresponding structures linking forms of government to conditions of the soul.

entries.label: Philosophers and Civic Society
entries.summary: While Socrates affirms that only true philosophers possess the unchanging vision required to govern, Adeimantus objects that common experience finds them useless or roguish. Socrates explains through the ship of state, unworthy imitators, and the sheltered remnant why authentic wisdom is exiled or corrupted in flawed cities.

entries.label: Curricular Path to Rule
entries.summary: Covering the cognitive assent to the faculties through solid geometry, carefully timed exposure to dialectic, progressive stages of education, and the civic cleansing required to institute the ideal city, Socrates outlines the training and inauguration of the guardians.

entries.label: Degenerate Soul Types
entries.summary: Socrates traces the progressive decline of individual character through the contentious timocrat, the avaricious oligarch driven by fear for possessions, and the democratic soul tossed by shifting, indiscriminate desires.

entries.label: The Tyrannical Soul and Rule
entries.summary: Examining the genesis of the tyrannical individual dominated by unlawful passions, Socrates details how absolute public rule intensifies misery and computes mathematically that the just king lives 729 times more pleasantly than the tyrant.

entries.label: The Philosopher and Society
entries.summary: Socrates examines the virtues inherent to true philosophers and the societal corruptions that divert gifted souls. He proposes a rigorous lifelong education to protect their nature and suggests the multitude will respect philosophy when its true, tranquil pursuit is revealed.

entries.label: Mathematical Sciences of Being
entries.summary: Arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and harmonics are presented as disciplines designed to elevate the intellect above sensory perception. Rather than serving purely practical or empirical aims, these studies compel the soul toward abstract truth, unchanging order, and eternal being.

entries.label: Decay into Oligarchy
entries.summary: The breakdown of the ideal commonwealth stems from breeding miscalculations, leading to factionalism and property division. As wealth becomes paramount, an oligarchy forms, breeding an impoverished and disenfranchised class of drones who eventually threaten the stability of the state.

entries.label: Democracy and Rise of Tyranny
entries.summary: Democracy emerges through popular rebellion, establishing widespread freedom, varied characters, and a tripartite social structure. Unchecked liberty ultimately gives rise to a demagogic champion who purges opponents, institutes martial rule, and subjugates the populace as a tyrant.

entries.label: Forms, Souls, and Imitation
entries.summary: Socrates depicts the soul's tripartite structure using a mythological composite figure and examines degrees of reality through the metaphor of three beds. Both accounts contrast true, rational essence with intermediate physical representations and base imitations.

entries.label: Nature of Justice & Self-Interest
entries.summary: These passages examine competing definitions of justice, contrasting Thrasymachus's claim that might makes right and Glaucon's social compact view with Socrates's refutations drawn from the analogy of the arts and the inherent weakness of evil. They also explore the demand to defend the intrinsic goodness of justice and happiness detached from external advantages.

entries.label: State Foundations & Common Good
entries.summary: This selection investigates the origin, purpose, and structural principles of the state, tracing how individual needs and the division of labour form a commonwealth whose objective is the happiness of the whole rather than any single faction. It connects the essential unity of justice and statecraft to modern reflections on the contingent, utility-based nature of property rights.

entries.label: Psychic Health, Truth & Culture
