entries.summary: These sections analyze the regulation of the soul and bodily health, distinguishing between intolerable internal deception and medicinal civic fictions while criticizing Plato's restrictive views on medicine and the arts. They assess the discipline needed to harmonize reason and spirited passion through education and contextually evaluate Plato's rejection of contemporary poetry.

entries.label: Dialectic & Philosophical Method
entries.summary: The commentary evaluates Platonic metaphysics and epistemology, identifying the dual aims of realizing and connecting abstract ideas while critiquing Plato's a priori logic for attempting to anticipate empirical science. It also compares the ancient contemplative ideal of unified wisdom with the modern division of scientific enquiry.

entries.label: Philosophy of History & Fate
entries.summary: This pair examines Plato's overarching frameworks of temporal and cosmic order, characterizing his sequence of deteriorating political regimes as an ideal progression of thought rather than historical chronology. It pairs this with his mythic reconciliation of cosmic necessity and human free will in the moral choice of lives.

entries.label: Debates on Justice in Book I
entries.summary: In Book I, Socrates and Thrasymachus contest the essence of justice and rule. Thrasymachus defines justice as the advantage of the stronger and portrays the ruler qua ruler as unerring, while Socrates counters that genuine arts serve their subjects, the just craftsman seeks no undue advantage, injustice breeds division, and justice constitutes the vital excellence of the soul.

entries.label: Nature of Goods and the State
entries.summary: Glaucon categorizes goods and presents the view of justice as a compromise arising from a social compact. In response, Socrates traces the origin of the state to human interdependence and establishes that civic efficiency relies on natural specialization and the division of labour.

entries.label: Theological and Poetic Education
entries.summary: Socrates establishes theological standards that portray the divine as unchangeable and the source solely of good, while classifying the modes of poetic narration. He further prescribes an educational program where simplicity, musical harmony, and physical training jointly attune the spirited and philosophical elements of the soul.

entries.label: Education and Civic Harmony
entries.summary: These passages focus on foundational policies for communal unity in the Republic, highlighting the primacy of character training over strict legislation, equal participation of women in governance and warfare, and the organic solidarity of citizens.

entries.label: Philosophy and Dialectic
entries.summary: This selection outlines the philosopher-ruler archetype and the epistemological journey required to attain true knowledge, encompassing the risks of philosophical corruption, the hierarchy of the Divided Line, and dialectic as the highest science.

entries.label: Regime Decline and Soul Orders
entries.summary: This sequence addresses Books VIII and IX, comparing the degenerative stages of constitutions and individual characters, the corresponding tripartite hierarchy of desires and pleasures, and the allegorical beast within the soul.

entries.label: Aesthetics and Character Growth
entries.summary: The commentary evaluates the role of artistic expression, music, and physical exercise in forming human nature, noting their capacity to harmonize reason and emotion when properly regulated.

entries.label: Critiques of Platonic Proposals
entries.summary: These discussions offer critical evaluations of Plato's radical social engineering, contrasting his proposals for female equality with commentary on the futility of breeding schemes, the necessity of the biological family, and the purely ideal nature of the state.

entries.label: Virtue, Duty, and the Soul
entries.summary: These passages establish the moral psychology of Book IV, arguing that duty and moral right take precedence over utilitarian calculations. Justice is defined as an internal harmony where the rational, spirited, and concupiscent faculties of the soul fulfill their proper functions.

entries.label: Epistemology and the Good
entries.summary: This sequence traces the central metaphysics and epistemology of Books V–VII, contrasting unerring knowledge of real being with opinion of contingent objects. It culminates in the Idea of the Good, illuminated through the analogy of the sun and the allegory of the cave's ascent from shadows to intellectual light.

entries.label: Ideal Governance and Analogy
entries.summary: These sections examine the practical and theoretical challenges of political order, contrasting the celestial pattern of the ideal city with the distrust faced by philosopher-statesmen. Commentary critiques Plato's assimilation of state to individual while evaluating his calls for simplicity in law, medicine, and preventive social governance.

entries.label: Heredity and Human Value
entries.summary: These texts critique Platonic biological engineering for reducing human relationships to animal breeding while ignoring spiritual affection and individual worth. They emphasize that while heredity transmits traits, human agency and moral will retain the power of prevention and character formation.

entries.label: Education and Transcendent Ideals
entries.summary: These reflections examine education as an ongoing conversion of the soul through dialectic toward transcendent principles. They explore how philosophical ideals—including the Idea of the Good, modern dual aspirations of progress and eternal life, and the Christian Divine Man—elevate human conduct above routine existence.

entries.label: Psychology & Opposites
entries.summary: Socrates lays down foundational principles regarding contrary states, distinguishing the intermediate neutrality of rest from genuine pleasure, formulating the non-contradiction principle for parts and wholes, and asserting the immortal endurance of the soul.

entries.label: Civic Unity & Shared Feeling
entries.summary: In Book V, Socrates defines civic cohesion as the paramount good of the commonwealth, likening the harmonious state to a single organism where injury to any part elicits shared joy and grief across the whole community.

entries.label: Forms, Faculties & Ideals
entries.summary: Socrates establishes that philosophers desire the entirety of wisdom, examining how singular Forms manifest across fluctuating sensory particulars, characterizing mental faculties by their sphere and results, and affirming ideals as valid evaluative standards irrespective of concrete realization.

entries.label: Education & Aesthetic Culture
entries.summary: Editorial notes examine Plato's pedagogical systems, detailing the tiered progression from music and gymnastics to advanced dialectics while highlighting the moral censorship and moderation required in art and melody.

entries.label: Civic Structure & Communism
entries.summary: Paratext commentary traces the composition of Plato's state between Spartan militarism and Athenian culture, analyzing how the communal abolition of private property and family aims to preserve civic cohesion across the dialogues.

entries.label: Dialectic, Theology & Good
entries.summary: Editorial commentary synthesizes Plato's supreme metaphysical concepts, outlining the perfection and unchanging truth of God, the ascent of dialectic beyond eristic hypotheses, and the transcendent Idea of the Good as the source of truth and being.

entries.label: Civic Order and Guardianship
entries.summary: Socrates establishes foundational principles for the just city, emphasizing the collective happiness of the entire community through proportionate class functioning, the preservation of education and music against innovation, the unifying civic harmony of temperance, and the assignment of public duties according to true capacity rather than bodily distinctions.

entries.label: Structure of the Soul and Desire
entries.summary: Socrates analyzes internal psychology by distinguishing the rational, spirited, and appetitive elements of the soul, while further categorizing appetites into necessary, natural desires versus dispensable, corruptive indulgences.

entries.label: Epistemology: Knowledge vs Opinion
entries.summary: Socrates distinguishes philosophers who grasp eternal, unchanging Forms from lovers of sights and sounds who focus on mutable particulars. By mapping knowledge to being and ignorance to non-being, he defines opinion as a distinct, intermediate faculty concerned with fluctuating phenomena.

entries.label: Book X: Soul, Fate, and Mimesis
entries.summary: Socrates demonstrates the deficiency of imitation relative to making and using, argues for the immortality of the soul on the basis that moral vice cannot extinguish it, and recounts the Myth of Er detailing the post-mortem judgement of deeds and the cosmic mechanism of Necessity's spindle.

entries.label: Editorial Synopses of Themes
entries.summary: Scholarly commentary synthesizes Plato's principal frameworks across the Republic, tracking the degenerative succession of civic constitutions matched to psychic disorders, the central role of justice as organic harmony, the rationale for censoring poetry, and the comprehensive development of Platonic psychology and eschatology.

entries.label: Civic and Psychic Harmony
entries.summary: Justice is defined at both civic and personal levels as each element performing its natural function without overstepping. When the tripartite soul is ordered under reason rather than unruly desires, internal harmony replaces the destructive effects of injustice.

entries.label: Philosopher and the State
entries.summary: Socrates argues that political suffering cannot end until philosophical wisdom and governance unite in the philosopher-king. However, existing cities fail to nurture this philosophic nature, leaving it estranged and degenerate without a matching ideal commonwealth.

entries.label: The Good and Epistemic Levels
entries.summary: The Idea of the Good is presented as the supreme source of truth and being, illustrated through the analogy of the sun. Epistemic reality is mapped via the Divided Line, showing dialectic ascending beyond ungrounded hypotheses to first principles, surpassing ordinary arts and mathematical sciences.

entries.label: Allegory of the Cave
entries.summary: Chained prisoners mistake fire-cast shadows on a subterranean wall for true reality until one is dragged into the open daylight. Gradually adapting from reflections to celestial bodies, the freed individual ultimately perceives the sun itself as the supreme cause of the visible realm.

entries.label: Knowledge, Pleasure, and Mimēsis
entries.summary: Because the philosopher commands experience alongside reason, his judgment prioritizing intellectual pleasure stands as uniquely valid. Conversely, imitative poets and artists lack true knowledge, producing works thrice removed from reality that deceive the senses and corrupt the soul.

entries.label: Soul Purity and Afterlife Choice
entries.summary: The soul's true nature is obscured in bodily existence like the encrusted sea-god Glaucus, becoming evident only through its philosophical kinship with the divine. In the afterlife, souls choose their subsequent incarnations freely, where a foundation in wisdom is critical to avoid catastrophic moral error.

entries.label: Education and the Ideal Ruler
entries.summary: Philosophic rule requires ascending from visible shadows to the Idea of the Good through dialectic and soul conversion. Having achieved intellectual vision and fourfold mental alignment, enlightened philosophers are obligated to return and draft laws for the commonwealth.

entries.label: Soul Health and Inner Harmony
entries.summary: Virtue functions as internal health and order, where true pleasure stems from unchanging truth rather than bodily replenishment. Wise individuals order their internal city according to divine rule and a heavenly pattern regardless of external circumstances.

entries.label: Regimes and Character Degeneration
entries.summary: State constitutions mirror the souls of their citizens across five distinct forms, showing how an insatiable pursuit of liberty in democracy gives birth to tyranny. A formal comparison concludes that the just, royal man is happiest, while the tyrannical man is the most miserable.

entries.label: Critique of Imitative Poetry
entries.summary: Imitative art appeals directly to the irrational, emotionally volatile parts of the soul, subverting inner governance. Because of an ancient quarrel between philosophy and poetry, poetic works must be excluded unless proven morally and politically beneficial.

entries.label: Eschatology and Virtue's Rewards
entries.summary: Having established the intrinsic worth of justice, Socrates restores the external honors and divine favor it earns during life. The mythic account of the soul's rebirth from the river of Unmindfulness culminates in a final plea to pursue virtue across this life and the next.

entries.label: Editorial and Structural Setup
entries.summary: Jowett presents the third edition translation and its extensive textual alterations alongside a structural overview charting the fivefold evolution of the dialogue and Socrates' pedagogical method.

entries.label: Book I Dialectic on Justice
entries.summary: Discussions and direct dialogue from Book I examine traditional maxims, ruler fallibility, and Thrasymachus's defense of injustice, culminating in Socrates' aporia and admission that he knows nothing.

entries.label: Book II Moral Foundations
entries.summary: Glaucon and Adeimantus challenge Socrates to defend justice for its intrinsic value, prompting the methodology of reading justice in the State before the individual and the selection of guardian natures combining spirit with gentleness.

entries.label: Guardian Culture and Discipline
entries.summary: Commentaries and Book III dialogue specify the education of the guardian class through rigorous censorship of poetry, restriction of musical instruments and modes, physical training, the myth of the metals, and communal living without private property.

entries.label: Philosophic Rule and Epistemology
entries.summary: Analyses center on the philosopher's role in the ideal commonwealth, detailing the mathematical curriculum of being, dialectic training, the allegory of the true pilot, and the necessary return of thinkers into civic affairs.

entries.label: Regime Decay and Tyrant's Misery
entries.summary: Discussions analyze the stepwise decline of constitutional regimes and human souls, the extreme misery and terror of the tyrannical character, and the mathematical formula contrasting royal happiness with tyrannical suffering.

entries.label: Utopian Lineage and Metaphysics
entries.summary: Commentary traces Platonic political philosophy across history—evaluating Spartan influences, cosmic calculations, and Pythagorean models while comparing the Republic to the Laws, Cicero, Augustine, More, and Campanella.

entries.label: Foundations of Justice
entries.summary: These texts focus on the foundational debates of Books I and II regarding the nature, origin, and value of justice. They contrast Thrasymachus's and Glaucon's conventionalist perspectives—depicting justice as power or mutual compromise—with Socrates's arguments establishing justice's intrinsic excellence and its emergence through human interdependence.

entries.label: Civic Order and Internal Duty
entries.summary: This sequence examines the structural harmony of the state and the internal constitution of the soul in Book IV. It highlights how the division of labour, civic unity, gender equality in governance, and the tripartite alignment of faculties establish justice as an overarching moral duty prioritized over utilitarian calculation.

entries.label: Poetic and Cultural Formation
entries.summary: Covering the regulation of poetry, music, and physical training, these selections address early moral and aesthetic education. They trace Socrates's strict censorship of theological myths alongside analytical appraisals of how simple harmony, literary forms, and disciplined bodily regimens properly attune the spirited and rational soul.

entries.label: Metaphysics and Dialectic
entries.summary: These clusters trace the core epistemological and metaphysical framework of Books V–VII. They outline the ascent from opinion to absolute being through the Divided Line, the Allegory of the Cave, and dialectic as the coping-stone of the sciences, while critically contrasting Platonic a priori methods with modern scientific inquiry.

entries.label: Critiques of Platonic Polity
entries.summary: These discussions evaluate Plato's radical social institutions and political analogies, scrutinizing his proposals for community of families, breeding schemes, and philosopher-rulers. Commentaries stress the necessity of the biological family, the spiritual dignity of individuals, and the gap between an earthly commonwealth and an ideal celestial pattern.

entries.label: Regimes, Destiny, and Cyclical History
entries.summary: This group explores Plato's temporal frameworks of constitutional decline and cosmic destiny across Books VIII–X. It pairs the psychological degeneration through timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny with the ancient cyclical conception of history and the moral responsibility of the soul choosing its life within necessity.

entries.label: Lifelong Education & Ideals
entries.summary: These texts consider education as an enduring conversion of the soul throughout life, driven by dialectical pursuit of transcendent standards. They examine how Platonic archetypes like the Good and parallel modern aspirations elevate human conduct and character above common routine.

entries.label: Foundations of Guardian Rule
entries.summary: Socrates details the selection, training, and communal obligations of the guardian class, emphasizing judicial wisdom, austerity, and proportional civic happiness over private luxuries or medical pampering.

entries.label: Communal Equality and Justice
entries.summary: These discussions define civic justice through distinct class duties, extend equal education and military roles to female guardians, and establish principles for regulated reproduction and inter-Hellenic conduct.

entries.label: Philosophers and Flawed States
entries.summary: Socrates addresses objections regarding the apparent uselessness or corruption of philosophers, using allegories such as the ship of state to contrast true contemplation of being with corrupted natures and unworthy imitators.

entries.label: Curriculum of Dialectic and Truth
entries.summary: The higher educational program directs future rulers from mathematical sciences and solid geometry through mature dialectic, culminating in the vision of the good required to govern the commonwealth.

entries.label: Civic and Character Degeneration
entries.summary: Tracing the decay of the ideal commonwealth through timocracy, oligarchy, and democracy, Socrates charts how unrestrained desires and factionalism produce drone classes, demagogic leaders, and tyrannical rule.

entries.label: Tyranny, Pleasure, and Reality
entries.summary: Socrates evaluates the misery of the tyrannical soul, contrasting base desires with pure painless pleasures like scent and distinguishing genuine essence from material copies and artistic imitations.

entries.label: Indices and Editorial Apparatus
entries.summary: Editorial notes, thematic indexes on virtue, rulers, and Homer, and scholarly commentary contextualize Plato's polity against historical Athenian and Spartan practices.

entries.label: Commentary on Plato's System
entries.summary: Scholarly paratext and editorial commentary analyze Plato's systemic frameworks across the Republic, addressing pedagogical tiers, censorship, civic communism, dialectical theology, and the structural analogies connecting constitutional decay with psychic corruption.

entries.label: Civic Unity, Forms, and Kingship
entries.summary: Socrates establishes civic cohesion through shared feeling, defines the epistemic divide between mutable opinion and intelligible Forms, and argues that political suffering cannot end until philosophical wisdom governs the state.

entries.label: Epistemology, Cave, and Dialectic
entries.summary: Through the analogies of the Sun, the Divided Line, and the Allegory of the Cave, Socrates traces the dialectical ascent to the supreme Idea of the Good and details the resulting obligation of enlightened rulers to govern.

entries.label: Psychic Order and Political Decay
entries.summary: Socrates articulates the tripartite division of the soul, contrasting internal harmony and virtue as health with unruly desires. This psychological balance is mapped onto civic constitutions to demonstrate how constitutional decay from aristocracy to tyranny mirrors escalating psychic misery.

entries.label: Mimesis, Immortality, and Er
entries.summary: Book X analyses reject imitative art as thrice removed from reality and corruptive of psychic reason, establish the immortality of the soul, and recount the Myth of Er to demonstrate the soul's posthumous judgement, cosmic necessity, and choice of destiny.

entries.label: Early Debates and Moral Roots
entries.summary: These clusters trace the dialectical debates of Books I and II over conventional versus intrinsic accounts of justice. Socrates counters the cynical challenges of Thrasymachus, Glaucon, and Adeimantus by shifting the inquiry toward political foundations and guardian nature.

entries.label: Civic Formation and Soul Order
entries.summary: These sections address guardian discipline, educational censorship, and communal regulations alongside the internal tripartite harmony of the soul in Books III and IV. Justice is identified as internal order and civic duty overarching utilitarian calculation.

entries.label: Epistemology, Dialectic & Form
entries.summary: This sequence focuses on the philosophical ascent through mathematics and dialectic to the Idea of the Good, along with the allegories of the Cave, Sun, and Divided Line. It highlights the philosopher's political duty, lifelong soul conversion, and the divergence between ancient speculation and modern method.

entries.label: Regime Decay and Soul Misery
entries.summary: Covering Books VIII–X, these clusters detail the cyclical devolution of constitutional regimes and human souls into the abject misery of tyranny. The discussions integrate Plato's ethical hierarchy of pleasures, cosmic numbers, and the soul's moral responsibility under necessity.

entries.label: Utopian Models and Lineage
entries.summary: These essays evaluate Plato's radical institutional proposals—such as community of property and wives—against historical models like Sparta and later utopian thinkers including Cicero, Augustine, More, and Campanella. Modern critiques emphasize the biological family, individual dignity, and the tension between celestial ideals and practical politics.

entries.label: Education and Guardian Polity
entries.summary: This sequence addresses the foundational upbringing and civic structure of the kallipolis, establishing strict censorship of myth, harmonious musical and gymnastic regimens, and rigorous tests for selecting guardians. It defines social justice as specialized non-interference, extends equal training and military duties to female guardians, and establishes communal living and regulated reproduction.

entries.label: Philosopher-Kings and Metaphysics
entries.summary: These discussions argue that ending civic suffering requires philosopher-kings, confronting public charges of philosophical uselessness through the ship of state allegory while identifying corrupting influences. They chart the epistemological ascent through the analogies of the Sun, Line, and Cave, and culminate in an advanced mathematical and dialectical curriculum designed to reveal the Idea of the Good.

entries.label: Constitutional and Psychic Decay
entries.summary: Tracing the stepwise decline of the ideal state through timocracy, oligarchy, democracy, and tyranny, these clusters map civic factionalism directly onto the corruption of the tripartite soul. They analyze the misery of the tyrannical man, distinguish between true and illusory pleasures, and emphasize internal harmony under rational rule.

entries.label: Scholarly Paratext and Indexes
entries.summary: These companion sections compile editorial commentary, thematic index entries, and transcription notes that contextualize Plato's philosophical polity. They examine the dialogue's pedagogical tiers, civic communism, dialectical theology, and historical contrasts with Athenian and Spartan institutions.

entries.label: Editorial Frames and Indexes
entries.summary: These clusters compile the overarching editorial framework of the edition, containing Jowett's structural preface, acknowledgments, textual revision histories, and extensive thematic indexes and transcription notes.

entries.label: Early Debates and Civic Design
entries.summary: This sequence moves from early dialectical inquiries into justice through foundational civic architecture, detailing guardian selection, censorship, education, and the psychological harmony of the state and individual.

entries.label: Metaphysics and Utopian Ideals
entries.summary: These discussions center on the philosopher-king paradox, the ascent to the Idea of the Good via the Sun, Line, and Cave allegories, and the institutional evaluation of Platonic utopianism against historical and later models.

entries.label: Regime Decline, Art, and Er
entries.summary: These sections examine the progressive devolution of polities and the soul from timocracy to tyranny, concluding with the repudiation of mimesis, the proof of the soul's immortality, and the eschatological vision of the Myth of Er.
